text:
**Short answer:** For a typical full-size fridge, get a pure sine wave power station with at least 1,300 W of surge output and about 1,400-2,000 Wh of capacity for a full day. About 1,000 Wh covers most of a day. Plan on roughly 2,800 Wh for two days.

**The three checks**

1. **Surge watts (the one that most often rules out a unit).** The compressor draws a brief startup spike, roughly 1,200-2,400 W on a household fridge. Choose a station whose surge rating is at least about 1,300 W ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator), [BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). Small units meant for phones and laptops often fail this check.
2. **Continuous watts.** A fridge typically runs at 100-250 W, which almost any 1,000 W-class station handles.
3. **Watt-hours.** The compressor cycles on only about 30-40% of the time, so average use is far below the running watts. Estimates range from about 41 W average for an efficient ENERGY STAR model to 50-70 Wh per hour for a more conservative case ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). Their estimated runtimes:
   - ~1,000 Wh: about 17 hours
   - ~2,000 Wh: about 33 hours

Also look for a pure sine wave inverter. Anker's guide notes that pure sine wave is strongly preferred for compressor motors ([Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)).

**To fine-tune for your fridge**
- Find the kWh/year on its yellow EnergyGuide label. Average watts = kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760. A large side-by-side with an ice maker can average about twice the efficient-model figure.
- Multiply the average watts by outage hours, divide by 0.85 for inverter losses, and add about 20% headroom ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- Add the watt-hours for anything else you want to run, such as a router or lights.
- Keep the door shut during the outage to cut usage.

**Options that fit**

| Need | Option | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ~Most of a day | [BLUETTI AC180](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W, 2,700 W peak) | BlackBox's top pick, seen at $399-699. I don't have a direct store link, so the link goes to their guide. |
| ~Most of a day | [Jackery Explorer 1000 v2](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) (1,070 Wh) | $499 listed; about 17 hours estimated. |
| ~24 hours or more | [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W, 3,000 W peak) | $699.99 after coupon on Anker's page. |
| ~24 hours or more, expandable | [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l) (2,048 Wh, 2,400 W, expandable to 8,192 Wh) | $899, or $854.05 with code AFF5OFF per Dealectric, which tested it on 2026-10-21. Check the final price at checkout. Dealectric earns an affiliate commission. |

Prices and stock change quickly. For example, one retailer listed the AC180P as sold out on Oct 15.

**Rule of thumb:** If outages in your area are usually under a day, a ~1,000-1,200 Wh unit is enough. If they run longer or you want margin, get 2,000 Wh or more. An expandable model like the AC200L lets you add capacity later. If you can't test your fridge's actual startup draw, favor a station with a generous surge rating.
